source_text:
Ἐγὼ γοῦν κἀκεῖνο φήσαιμ᾿ ἄν· ἐπειδὴ τὰ μὲν ἐντός ἐστι τῆς ψυχῆς, τὰ δὲ ἐκτός, κἂν μὲν ἡ ψυχὴ χρῆται καλῶς. καλὰ καὶ ταῦτα δοκεῖ, ἐὰν δὲ πονηρῶς. πονηρά, ὁ κελεύων ἀπαλλοτριοῦν τὰ ὑπάρχοντα π[ρ]ότερον ταῦτα παραιτεῖται ὧν ἀναιρεθέντων ἔτι τὰ πάθη μένει, ἢ ἐκεῖνα μᾶλλον ὧν ἀναιρεθέντων καὶ τὰ κτήματα χρήσιμα γίνεται; ὁ τοίνυν ἀποβαλὼν τὴν κοσμικὴν περιουσίαν ἔτι δύναται πλουτεῖν τῶν παθῶν καὶ τῆς ὕλης μὴ παρούσης· ἡ γάρ τοι διάθεσις τὸ αὑτῆς ἐνεργεῖ καὶ τὸν λογισμὸν ἄγχει καὶ πιέζει καὶ φλεγμαίνει ταῖς συντρόφοις ἐπιθυμίαις· οὐδὲν οὖν προὔργου γέγονεν αὐτῷ πτωχεύειν χρημάτων πλουτοῦντι τῶν παθῶν. οὐ γὰρ τὰ ἀπόβλητα ἀπέβαλεν, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀδιάφορα, καὶ τῶν μὲν ὑπηρετικῶν ἑαυτὸν περιέκοψεν, ἐξέκαυσε δὲ τὴν ὕλην τῆς κακίας τὴν ἔμφυτον τῇ τῶν ἐκτὸς ἀπορίᾳ. ἀποτακτέον οὖν τοῖς ὑπάρχουσι τοῖς βλαβεροῖς. οὐχὶ τοῖς ἐὰν ἐπίστηταί τις τὴν ὀρθὴν χρῆσιν καὶ συνωφελεῖν δυναμένοις. ὠφελεῖ δὲ τὰ μετὰ φρονήσεως καὶ σωφροσύνης καὶ εὐσεβείας οἰκονομούμενα, ἀπωστέα δὲ τὰ ἐπιζήμια· τὰ δὲ ἐκτὸς οὐ βλάπτει.
Οὕτως οὖν ὁ κύριος καὶ τὴν τῶν ἐκτὸς χρείαν εἰσάγει.
thought_title: Possessions are indifferent; the passions are what must be renounced
orientation: Clement is explaining that the command to sell one's possessions refers to the passions of the soul, not to external goods, which are indifferent in themselves.
pass_a_gloss: I for my part would say that too: since some things are within the soul, and some things are outside, and if the soul uses them well, these things also seem good, but if badly, evil, does the one who commands to alienate one's possessions reject these things first, after whose removal the passions still remain, or rather those things after whose removal the possessions also become useful? The one who has thrown away worldly abundance can still be rich in passions even when the material is not present; for the disposition works its own work and chokes and oppresses the reasoning and burns with its inborn desires. It has therefore been of no advantage to him to be poor in money while being rich in passions. For he has not thrown away the things that should be thrown away, but the indifferent things, and he has cut himself off from the things that serve him, but he has kindled the material of evil that is innate by the lack of external things. One must therefore renounce the possessions that are harmful, not those which, if someone understands the right use, can also help. And the things managed with prudence and self-control and piety help, but the things that cause loss must be thrust away; but external things do not harm. Thus then the Lord also introduces the need for external things.

lemmas.gloss: to alienate, to make another's, to renounce
to reject, to ask to be excused from
to throw away, to cast off
indifferent things, things neither good nor evil
one must renounce, one must bid farewell to
must be thrust away, must be repelled

choices.why: The verb means to make something another's, to estrange or transfer; 'alienate' preserves the legal and dispossessive force while avoiding the banned 'property' for ὑπάρχοντα.
This is a technical Stoic term for things neither good nor evil in themselves; Clement uses it precisely to argue that external goods are morally neutral.
The term denotes a settled state or condition of the soul; 'disposition' captures the habitual orientation that Clement says works its own work even without external material.
The verbal adjective expresses necessity; 'renounce' matches the ascetic force of ἀποτάσσω, which means to bid farewell to or detach from.
ἐπιζήμιος means harmful or causing damage; rendering it as 'things that cause loss' keeps the economic register that fits the discussion of possessions.

pass_b_english: I myself would say this as well. Since some things are within the soul and others are outside it, if the soul uses them well, these too appear good, but if badly, they appear evil. Does the one who commands us to alienate our possessions reject these first—the things whose removal still leaves the passions in place—or rather those things whose removal makes even possessions useful? For the person who has thrown away his worldly wealth can still be rich in passions even when the material is absent. His disposition does its own work: it chokes and presses his reasoning and burns with the desires that have grown up with him. So it has done him no good to become poor in money while he is rich in passions. He has not thrown away what should be thrown away, but only indifferent things. He has cut himself off from what could serve him, and by his lack of outward things he has kindled the innate fuel of evil. One must therefore renounce the possessions that cause harm, not those that can also help if someone understands their right use. Things managed with wisdom, self-control, and reverence do good, but the things that cause loss must be thrust away. Outward things do not harm.
So then the Lord also introduces the need for outward things.

problems.why: κοσμικὴ περιουσία means worldly abundance/wealth, not 'surplus'; the point is total worldly wealth, not excess.
problems.ruling: Greek 'κοσμικὴν περιουσίαν' means worldly property/wealth, not 'surplus'; translation adds nuance of excess, altering meaning.

fixed: Changed 'worldly surplus' to 'worldly wealth' because κοσμικὴ περιουσία means worldly abundance/wealth, not surplus.
